exercicios.enunciado: Complete a frase.
exercicios.frase: It [must] be the exchange rate. I'm almost sure.

exercicios.enunciado: Complete a frase.
exercicios.frase: It [might] be the price per night — I'm not sure.

exercicios.enunciado: Complete a frase.
exercicios.frase: Paulo isn't answering. His plane left at nine. He [must] be on the plane.

exercicios.enunciado: "Não pode ser!" Em inglês:
exercicios.explicacao: Na dedução, o contrário de must é can't.

exercicios.enunciado: "You must wear a helmet." Here, must means…
"It must be the exchange rate." Here, must means…
Deve ser um erro.

exercicios.frase: This is Sílvia. The budget was fifty-seven million kwanzas. We spent sixty-five and a half.
exercicios.enunciado: How much did they spend?

opcoes.texto: sixty-five and a half million kwanzas

exercicios.frase: It must be the exchange rate. That can't be right.
exercicios.enunciado: Ouça e repita: "must" fraco, "can't" forte.
Make four guesses about your office or your home: a colleague who isn't there, a noise, a price, and a number on a document.
exercicios.frase: can't
exercicios.resposta: My colleague João isn't here today. He must be ill — he's never late. That noise outside might be the generator. This printer can't be new — it's so slow! And the electricity bill is double. That can't be right.

exercicios.enunciado: What's the best way to check a strange number on an invoice?
exercicios.frase: must
exercicios.resposta: First, I compare it with the last invoice. If the number is very different, it must be a mistake, or the price has changed. Then I call the supplier and ask them to explain it in writing.

exercicios.enunciado: "Costs went up to 65 million." The number 65 million is…
¼ in English is…

exercicios.frase: I'm Sílvia. The kwanza has fallen by about ten percent against the dollar.
exercicios.enunciado: How much has the kwanza fallen?

exercicios.frase: This is Sílvia. Hotel prices in Lobito rose from fifty-five thousand to sixty-five thousand kwanzas a night.
exercicios.enunciado: How much is a night now?

exercicios.frase: Fifteen percent. Fifty percent. Thirteen thousand. Thirty thousand.
exercicios.enunciado: Ouça e repita: -teen com acento no fim, -ty no princípio.
How have prices changed where you live in the last year? Talk about three things, with numbers and "went up by" or "rose to".
exercicios.frase: went up
exercicios.resposta: In my city, prices have gone up a lot this year. A bag of rice went up from five thousand to six thousand kwanzas — a rise of twenty percent. The taxi to my office rose to one thousand kwanzas. Only my rent stayed the same.

exercicios.enunciado: Which price rise is the hardest for families: food, transport or school? Why?
exercicios.frase: because
exercicios.resposta: In my view, food is the hardest, because families can't cut down on it. You can walk instead of taking a taxi, but you can't stop eating! And food prices went up by about twenty percent where I live.

exercicios.enunciado: Complete a frase.

opcoes.texto: Will you be using the meeting room this afternoon?
You use the meeting room this afternoon?
Use the meeting room this afternoon?

exercicios.enunciado: "This time next week, I'll be presenting the budget." At that moment, Nuno…

exercicios.enunciado: Choose the correct sentence.

I'll working at the bank all day on Monday.
I be working at the bank all day on Monday.

exercicios.enunciado: Amanhã a esta hora, vou estar a viajar para Benguela.
exercicios.resposta: This time tomorrow, I'll be travelling to Benguela.

exercicios.frase: This is Paulo. We'll be finishing the two rooms here tomorrow, and then the engineer will be flying to Lobito on Friday.
exercicios.enunciado: When will the engineer be flying to Lobito?

exercicios.frase: Will you be using the car on Monday?
exercicios.enunciado: Ouça e repita, com "will you be" ligado.
Imagine it's this time next week. What will you be doing in the morning, at lunchtime and in the evening?
exercicios.frase: I'll be
exercicios.resposta: This time next week, I'll be travelling to Benguela for a training course. At lunchtime, I'll probably be eating fish with my colleagues by the sea. And in the evening, I'll be studying English in my hotel room.

exercicios.enunciado: Do you plan your week in detail, or do you prefer to decide day by day? Why?
exercicios.frase: plan
exercicios.resposta: I plan my week in detail, because I have a lot of meetings. On Sunday evening I check my calendar, so on Monday I know what I'll be doing every day. But I always leave some time free for problems.

exercicios.frase: I'm Joana. Last year I took out a small loan to buy more stock, and I'm still paying it back.
exercicios.enunciado: What is Joana still doing?

exercicios.frase: Share, change, budget. Cash, much, charge.
exercicios.enunciado: Ouça e repita os três sons.
How do you manage money at home or at work? Talk about a budget, one thing you cut down on, and something you set aside.
exercicios.frase: set aside
exercicios.resposta: At home, we make a budget every month. This year, food prices went up, so we cut down on eating out. And we set aside ten percent of our salaries for our children's school fees in September.

exercicios.enunciado: Is it a good idea to take out a loan to buy a car? Why?
exercicios.frase: loan
exercicios.resposta: It depends. If you need the car for work, a loan can be a good idea. But interest rates are very high, so you pay back much more than the price of the car. I prefer to set aside money and buy a cheaper car.

licoes.titulo: Real English: Where does the money go?
licoes.objectivo: Identificar os números, a tendência e a opinião em quatro conversas sobre preços e poupança.

exercicios.frase: I'm Esperança. The price of my taxis went up by half, to three thousand kwanzas a day.
exercicios.enunciado: How much do Esperança's taxis cost a day now?

exercicios.frase: This is Esperança. Now I share a car with two colleagues, and we pay for the fuel together.
exercicios.enunciado: How does Esperança save money now?

opcoes.texto: She shares a car with two colleagues.

exercicios.frase: I'm Kevin. Part of my salary is in pounds, so when the kwanza falls, my rent costs me less.
exercicios.enunciado: Why is a falling kwanza good news for Kevin?

opcoes.texto: Part of his salary is in pounds.
His rent went down in kwanzas.

exercicios.frase: This is Patrick. We've cut down on fuel by about fifteen percent since January.
exercicios.enunciado: How much did Patrick's company cut down on fuel?

exercicios.frase: I'm Joana. My problem is cash flow. My suppliers want to be paid in advance.
exercicios.enunciado: What is Joana's main problem?

exercicios.frase: This is Joana. Next year I'll be looking for a supplier who accepts instalments.
exercicios.enunciado: What will Joana be looking for next year?
Each person in the four conversations gives…

opcoes.texto: a number, a trend and an opinion

exercicios.enunciado: Kevin says: "It can't be easy for my colleagues." He thinks…

exercicios.frase: The price went up by half.
exercicios.enunciado: Ouça e repita em voz alta.

exercicios.frase: I'm still paying it back.
exercicios.enunciado: Ouça e repita em voz alta.
Whose situation is most like yours? Explain why, with one number and one opinion.
exercicios.frase: like
exercicios.resposta: My situation is most like Esperança's. My bus fare went up from two hundred to three hundred kwanzas this year — a rise of fifty percent. So now I share a car with my neighbour. In my view, companies should organise transport for their staff.

exercicios.enunciado: Patrick says most companies waste money on bad planning, not on salaries. Do you agree? Why?
exercicios.frase: agree
exercicios.resposta: I partly agree. Bad planning costs a lot — for example, lorries that travel empty. But some companies also waste money on expensive offices and cars. In my view, good planning is the cheapest way to cut costs.

exercicios.enunciado: What is Nuno's first proposal?

opcoes.texto: to pay for the equipment when they sign the contract

exercicios.frase: This is David. If we add ten percent, our price will be higher than our competitors', and we might lose the contract.
exercicios.enunciado: Why does David refuse the ten percent?

exercicios.frase: Fifteen percent over budget — not fifty!
exercicios.enunciado: Ouça e repita, com o acento certo em "fifteen" e em "fifty".
Explain to your director: a training event cost 2.5 million kwanzas, not 2 million; the room stayed the same; food went up by 30%; ten more people came. Propose one cut.
exercicios.frase: propose
exercicios.resposta: The training cost two and a half million kwanzas — about twenty-five percent over budget. The room stayed the same. The food went up by thirty percent, and ten more people came. For the next event, I propose a registration deadline.

exercicios.enunciado: Explain this table in English: "Despesas do escritório — 1.º trimestre (mil Kz). Electricidade: 450 → 600 (+33%). Internet: 300 → 300 (0%). Papel e consumíveis: 200 → 150 (−25%)."
exercicios.frase: went up
exercicios.resposta: It shows our office costs for the first three months. Electricity went up from four hundred and fifty to six hundred thousand kwanzas — an increase of a third. The internet stayed the same. And paper and supplies went down by a quarter.
exercicios.contexto: Mediação: o que importa na tabela.

exercicios.frase: This is David. Five percent I can accept. Send me a summary today.
exercicios.enunciado: What does David accept?
How have prices changed where you live, and how do you save money?
exercicios.frase: save
exercicios.resposta: Prices have gone up a lot. Food rose by about twenty percent, and my bus fare went up from two hundred to three hundred kwanzas. To save money, I cook at home, I share a car with a colleague, and I set aside ten percent of my salary every month.

exercicios.enunciado: Your colleague says the electricity bill is double this month. Make two guesses.
exercicios.frase: must
exercicios.resposta: That can't be right — we didn't use more electricity. It must be a mistake. Or it might be the new price: I think the rates went up in January.
